column1: # JOACHIM PETER LEIBHOLZ'S BIRTH IS FOUND, AND THE MARRIAGE ROW 242 WANTED IS NOT THE ONE THAT IS THERE.
# Berliner Adressbuch 1903 (ZLB 34115495) and Landesarchiv Berlin LABSA, Namensverzeichnisse zum
# Geburten- and Heiratsregister, Standesamt Charlottenburg I and II. Row 242. Read 11 October 2026.
# WHY IT WAS RUN. The Victorian death index names Joachim Peter Leibholz's father as WILLIAM
# LEIBHOLZ and his mother as NANETTE née NETTER. Row 242 proposed the Berlin marriage indexes for a
# Leibholz-Netter marriage before 1903 and called itself "the best scoped and the only one worth
# running by eye". The scoping turned out to be wrong in a useful way and the row's own instrument
# was not the one that paid.
field
# ---------------- FIRST, THE SCOPING, WHICH COST ONE PAGE OF A DIRECTORY ----------------
*** WILLIAM LEIBHOLZ IS THE ONLY LEIBHOLZ IN CHARLOTTENBURG IN 1903, AND THE DIRECTORY GIVES HIS HOUSE ***
column2: WILLIAM, Fabrkbes., CHARLOTTENBURG, JOACHIMSTHALERSTR. 7. 8 II. (Tel. Charl. 1706.) — a FABRIKBESITZER, a factory owner, in the Berliner Adressbuch of 1903. The other twelve Leibholz entries in that volume are every one of them in Berlin proper: Rungestr, Alexanderstr, Unter den Linden, Ritterstr, Alte Jakobstr, Elbingerstr, Bergmannstr, Kurfürstendamm 28, Jostystr, Katharinenstr, Rosenstr and one widow. NOT ONE OTHER IS IN CHARLOTTENBURG.

column1: which fixes the registry office without guessing
column2: Joachimsthaler Straße lies in the district of STANDESAMT CHARLOTTENBURG I. Joachim Peter was born 20 AUGUST 1903. So his birth is registered at Charlottenburg I, and that is where to look — one volume rather than seventeen offices.

column1: and the row's premise is confirmed on the way
column2: this archive's Adressbuch notes already held a WILLIAM LEIBHOLZ, Generaldirektor and STADTRAT in 1920 and "William, Kaufm., W15 Kurfürstendamm 169" in 1913. 1903 puts the same man in Charlottenburg as a factory owner, between the two.

column1: # ---------------- AND THE BIRTH ENTRY IS THERE, FIRST TRY ----------------
*** LEIBHOLZ · JOACHIM PETER · 20.8. · 875 ***
column2: STANDESAMT CHARLOTTENBURG I, GEBURTSREGISTER 1903, NR. 875. P Rep. 551 Nr. 526, the 1903 birth index, 82 pages, read at the page image under the month-8 heading of the L block. The surname, both forenames, the day and the register number are all unambiguous at 1.6x and were checked again at the row.

column1: what the index does and does not give
column2: it gives the child, the day, the month and the REGISTER NUMBER, and nothing else — the "Zugehörigkeit der Eltern zu einer Kirche" column is blank for him and for everyone on the page. IT DOES NOT NAME THE PARENTS. *** THE ENTRY ITSELF, CHARLOTTENBURG I 1903 NR. 875, WOULD NAME THE MOTHER WITH HER MAIDEN NAME, *** and that is the document that settles whether she was Nanette née Netter. It is a certificate order and it is DAVID'S PURCHASE, not mine.

column1: why this matters beyond one date
column2: Joachim Peter is the MELBOURNE lane — sailed on the ANCHISES in 1939, landed 12 June, naturalised at South Yarra 27 July 1944 with previous nationality STATELESS, six files in the National Archives of Australia and none of them scanned. The archive has had his birth date from an Australian death index for weeks. IT NOW HAS THE GERMAN REGISTRATION BEHIND IT: an office, a year and a number.

column1: # ---------------- NOW THE MARRIAGE, AND THE ANSWER IS NOT THE ONE THE ROW EXPECTED ----------------
*** CHARLOTTENBURG I, MARRIAGES 1898 TO 1903, HOLDS EXACTLY ONE LEIBHOLZ — AND THE SPOUSE IS NOT A NETTER ***
column2: LEIBHOLZ | FRIEDLAENDER | 42. — STANDESAMT CHARLOTTENBURG I, HEIRATSREGISTER 1902, NR. 42, read at the page image in P Rep. 551 Nr. 462 under the 1902 heading of the L block, and zoomed to settle it. The whole L block of both volumes was read: P Rep. 551 Nr. 461 (1898-1900, pages 41-47) and Nr. 462 (1901-1903, pages 78-87). NO OTHER LEIBHOLZ IN SIX YEARS.

column1: and Charlottenburg II is clear for 1900 to 1903
column2: P Rep. 553 Nr. 528 (1900-1901, L block pages 40-45) and Nr. 529 (1902-1903, L block pages 41-45), both read at the image. NO LEIBHOLZ IN EITHER.

column1: *** WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH ***
column2: A 1902 marriage at Charlottenburg I and a birth in the same office in August 1903 is the right shape, and William is the only Leibholz in the borough. BUT THE INDEX GIVES SURNAMES ONLY — no forenames, and no indication of which party is the groom. The same page carries "Leistikow geb. Marschalk | Heimann", a woman indexed under L with her husband opposite, so A MISS LEIBHOLZ MARRYING A MR FRIEDLAENDER WOULD LOOK IDENTICAL. NOTHING HERE IS CLAIMED AS WILLIAM'S MARRIAGE.

column1: and the row's own expectation is now a question rather than an assumption
column2: the row was looking for LEIBHOLZ x NETTER. Six years of Charlottenburg I and four of Charlottenburg II contain no such marriage. THREE READINGS ARE POSSIBLE AND THIS ARCHIVE PICKS NONE: the 1902 Friedlaender marriage is William's and the Australian index's "Netter" is wrong; or William married Nanette Netter elsewhere or earlier and the Friedlaender marriage is another family's; or Netter is right and the marriage is in one of the offices not read.

column1: THE AUSTRALIAN INDEX IS THE WEAKEST DOCUMENT IN THIS CHAIN AND THAT SHOULD BE SAID
column2: a Victorian death index entry records what an informant said about a man's parents decades later, in another country and another language. THE SAME CLASS OF SOURCE WAS WRONG TWICE TODAY in a different family — a Page of Testimony missed a birth day and a death year that official lists got right. "Nanette née Netter" is a lead, not a fact, and the only thing that will settle it is Charlottenburg I 1903 Nr. 875.

column1: # ---------------- WHAT IS NOT READ, SO NOBODY THINKS IT IS ----------------
the unread marriage volumes, named
column2: Charlottenburg II 1898-1899 (P Rep. 553 Nr. 527) · Standesamt Charlottenburg undivided, 1893-1895 (P Rep. 550 Nr. 537) and 1896-1897 (Nr. 538), and the four earlier volumes back to 1874 · AND EVERY ONE OF STANDESAMT BERLIN I TO XIII, which is where the marriage would be if the couple lived in the city before moving out to Charlottenburg. The row's estimate of "perhaps twenty-five image reads" was about right for Charlottenburg and is a large underestimate for Berlin.

column1: and the cheap thing to do before any of that
column2: READ THE BIRTH ENTRY. One certificate names the mother, her maiden name and usually her birthplace, and it decides which of the three readings above is the true one. Everything else is reading index volumes against a surname that may be wrong.

column1: the indexes are image-only and were read as such
column2: LABSA's marriage and birth indexes carry no usable text layer — the 1903 Charlottenburg I birth index scores ZERO control names in its first thirty pages. Every finding above was read at the page image, and the two that the argument turns on, the birth row and the marriage row, were magnified and read twice.
